reading-review/paper-vs-screen.claim: Reading on paper yields better comprehension than reading the same text on a screen, especially for expository text read under time limits.

reading-review/automation-bias.claim: People reviewing automated or AI output accept its errors at elevated rates, both acting on wrong outputs (commission) and missing unflagged problems (omission). Interventions that force active evaluation reduce this overreliance.
reading-review/automation-bias.construct: automation bias and complacency; cognitive forcing
reading-review/automation-bias.suggested_rewording: People reviewing automated or AI output accept its errors at elevated rates, both acting on wrong outputs and missing unflagged problems; training and instructions do not prevent this, while design steps that force evaluation of each output reduced overreliance on AI in one experiment. (B for the first clause; C for the last)

reading-review/proofreading-marks.claim: A fixed, shared set of marks, each mapped to one editing action, is used reliably by writers and editors to communicate corrections on paper.
reading-review/proofreading-marks.construct: proofreaders' marks as a mark → action convention

reading-review/consistent-mapping.claim: Keeping each mark's or colour's meaning constant across contexts leads to faster, more accurate use than mappings that change with context, which provoke mode errors.
reading-review/consistent-mapping.construct: consistent vs varied mapping (automaticity); mode errors

return-checklist.helps: when a return has steps that are easy to forget; a checklist is meant to catch omissions, but the checklist evidence comes from clinical and cockpit procedures, not from sending pages back
return-checklist.backfires: when boxes get ticked without the steps being done

sheet.helps: when an expository text has to be understood, not skimmed: reading on paper gives slightly better comprehension than reading on screen, a small effect, largest for informational text
sheet.backfires: when the job is hunting for typos and slips, which the one error-detection study found easier on screen, or when the page is read without actively checking each point, which lets an AI draft's errors through

proof-page.helps: when an AI draft needs checking point by point: a number and a margin on every paragraph invite an active judgement on each, and paper gives slightly better comprehension of expository text
proof-page.backfires: when marking turns into rubber-stamping every paragraph, or when the job is catching surface typos, which one study found easier on screen

proof.helps: when an AI draft needs checking point by point: marking every paragraph forces an active judgement on each, which reduced overreliance on AI in one experiment, and paper gives slightly better comprehension of expository text; the mark conventions themselves are untested craft
proof.backfires: when marking turns into rubber-stamping, when the forcing step feels onerous enough to skip (users rated the most effective forcing designs least favourably), or when the job is catching surface errors, which one study found easier on screen

proof-actions.helps: when every mark keeps one meaning on every page, following the long practice of proofreaders' marks; whether fixed marks are used reliably has not been tested
proof-actions.backfires: when a mark's or colour's meaning shifts between pages or contexts, which invites mode errors even in trained users
